stem: A student using the passage to argue that NAFTA helped all American workers equally should be most cautious because the passage

rationales.A: The passage centers on Clinton, who signed the agreement and argued it would create jobs.
rationales.B: Canada is named in the first sentence, as one of the three countries in the agreement.
rationales.C: The passage was written at the signing, when the jobs and the factory moves were still promises and warnings, not results.
rationales.D: The passage comes from the signing in December 1993. Background: NAFTA was replaced only in 2020.
rationales.general:
1. Ask when the passage was written: at the signing, in December 1993.
2. At a signing, nobody knows the results yet — there are only promises on one side and warnings on the other.
3. So the passage can show what people hoped and feared, but not who actually gained.
4. A claim about equal help needs evidence from after the fact, not from the ceremony.
Remember: a ribbon-cutting tells you the promise, never the payoff.

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of President Bill Clinton's remarks on signing the North American Free Trade Agreement, December 8, 1993. Post-1929 material is paraphrased, not quoted.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of President Bill Clinton's remarks on signing the North American Free Trade Agreement, December 8, 1993: Clinton said the agreement would tear down trade barriers among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, letting American goods, services, and investment move freely across borders. He argued that open trade would create American jobs by opening new markets, even as critics warned that factories would move to Mexico in search of cheaper labor.
